newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea reduces death penalty on Chinese mutineers.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea reduces death penalty on Chinese mutineers.

text.p: A South Korean High Court on Friday commuted death sentences for five of six mainland Chinese seamen of Korean descent for murdering the captain of a Korean fishing vessel and 10 crew members, a court official said.
The court confirmed the death sentence on the sixth seaman, who was convicted as the ringleader, the official said. The sentences for the other five were commuted to life imprisonment.
The six had appealed against death sentences handed down in December by a criminal court in the port city of Pusan.

The court found them guilty of murdering the South Korean captain of a tuna boat along with three Indonesians, six South Koreans and an ethnic Korean Chinese in a mutiny in the South Pacific. Prosecutors said the mutiny was apparently sparked by harsh working conditions.
In addition to the mutineers, one South Korean navigator and six Indonesians survived the tragedy last August. The mutineers dumped the bodies overboard, according to police.
The case came to light when Japanese maritime police found the Pescamar No. 15 drifting without fuel south of Japan.
The judge in charge of the case said he commuted the sentence for the five seamen taking into account their harsh lives.
"They worked on the Korean ship to escape poverty in China," said judge Kim Jin-ki. "The decision was also an effort to resolve tensions between South Korea and the ethnic Korean community in China."
The number of ethnic Koreans coming to work in South Korea from China has increased in recent years, and many have complained of exploitation by their Korean employers.
Separately on Thursday, two vessels smuggling 106 Chinese were intercepted by the coast guard. The Chinese nationals will be returned to China after an investigation, immigration officials said.

The mutiny occurred after the captain radioed that he was heading for Samoa in the South Pacific to replace rebellious crewmen. Police said the Honduras-registered, 254-gross-ton vessel was later heading for China when its engines stopped.
South Korea's deep sea fishing fleet has hired increasing numbers of foreign crew because of rising wages at home.
